chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from al-'Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

A woman came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said, 'Marry me off.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Who will have her?' A man stood up and said, 'I will, O Messenger of Allah, marry her to me.' He asked, 'What will you give her?' He said, 'I have nothing.' He said, 'No.' She repeated, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) repeated, but no one else stood up except that man. Then she repeated again, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said on the third time, 'Do you know something of the Quran?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'I have married you off on what you know of the Quran. Teach it to her.'
The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And the marriage of Shighar is valid.

key_terms.شغار: A form of marriage where dowry is omitted, often involving an exchange
key_terms.مهر: Dowry given by the husband to the wife

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on using Quranic knowledge as a dowry in marriage?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the principle that knowledge of the Quran can serve as a valid dowry (mahr), reflecting the high value placed on religious education in early Shia jurisprudence. While the Prophet accepted this minimal form of compensation for a man with no material wealth, the Sheikh clarifies that this specific precedent validates the permissibility of *Shighar* (marriage without explicit monetary dowry) rather than negating the requirement of dowry entirely. This narration is frequently cited by scholars to demonstrate the flexibility of the marriage contract in accommodating varying socioeconomic conditions.
